runs.text: couſa ſe apreße, deſejo apreßarme ainda q̃ ſe-

lines.note: Continues the previous page’s maxim about hastening a good event: the speaker wishes to hurry, even if only by a short time. Couſa repeats the f388 catchword; the whole row is an indented Portuguese continuation, not a new entry.

runs.text: ja hum quarto, ou mea hora.

lines.note: Ja completes ſe-ja, followed by a quarter or half an hour. The printed mea is the historical form and is not regularized to meia.

runs.text: Bom dia, & ditoſo, ou bem eſ-

lines.note: Qichinichi means an auspicious day. Bom dia, ditoſo and bem eſ- describe a good, fortunate, well-begun day, rather than merely a greeting.
Treado completes eſtreado, the final characterization of the auspicious day. This short continuation closes Qichinichi.
Qichirei is a good precedent or usage, paraphrased by yoki tameshi. The scan joins Qichirei as one word; the Portuguese custume and its provisional italic st classification are preserved.

runs.text: Cortinas, ou panos ricos de armar que

lines.note: Qichǒ denotes a curtained furnishing, described as curtains or rich hanging cloths. The caron over o is visible and the sentence continues with the supporting framework.
Explains that these hangings were formerly arranged over a wooden frame. Armauão and madeiramento are retained as historical Portuguese, not modernized.

runs.text: que ſe podia menear, ou mudar como Biǒbus.

lines.note: The framework could be moved or shifted like folding screens. Enlargement reads Biǒbus with a caron, not OCR Bibhus; the Japanese-derived term is embedded in an otherwise italic Portuguese explanation.
This Qichǒ is hunger, paraphrased by fidarui, hungry. The Portuguese begins barriga fa-, a hungry belly, and does not refer to the furnishing above.
Minta completes faminta. The final S. is an upright usage label outside the italic Portuguese gloss. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Qichô is returning to one’s country. The scan has Tornar, not Tomar, and the repeated verb Qichôſuru also bears the circumflex; its compact spelling is retained.

runs.text: Idem. Como os que vão à China, ou aos Luçoẽs

lines.note: The same meaning is illustrated by people who go to China or Luzon. Luçoẽs is the printed historical geographical name and retains its visible tilde carrier.
Completes the example: they return to Japan. The initial in Iapão is capital I, not a lowercase l; this return from abroad is contrasted with the later Qicocu entry.
Qichǒmen here is an architectural treatment of rounded or blunted corners, not the modern personality adjective. The scan reads Cantos, restoring the t lost by OCR, and preserves rodondos.

runs.text: ſe fazem como ſeparados ẽ algũas Faxiras qua-

lines.note: The corners are formed as distinct edges on certain square pillars. Faxiras, from hashira with a Portuguese plural ending, occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is retained in the printed italic setting.
Dradas completes quadradas. Qichǒmenuo toru illustrates making the architectural corner treatment; the following Di- is the italic beginning of Portuguese Diuidir, not a Japanese fragment.

runs.text: uidir eſtes cantos, ou bordas pera ſe vruxarẽ,

lines.note: Completes Diuidir: shaping or separating these corners and edges so they can be lacquered. Enlargement supports vruxarẽ, the Japanese-derived lacquer verb, rather than OCR vrucarẽ; the abbreviated ending remains unexpanded.
Ornarem completes the purpose of the corner treatment, ornamenting the members. It belongs to the architectural Qichǒmen sense, not to the following honorific address.

Qicô is an honorific for the addressee, paraphrased by an honored lord. The scan has Qicô rather than Qacô and voſſa merce rather than the corrupted OCR vaſa meree; the paired long-s shapes were enlarged for inspection.
Senhoria extends the list of honorific equivalents. The upright S. stands outside the italic gloss as the usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Certa fruita que ſe dà em hũs eſpinhos

lines.note: This Qicocu is a medicinal fruit produced on a thorny plant. The scan’s dà and hũs retain their visible accent and abbreviation, without adding a modern botanical identification.
The fruit is said to serve as a remedy. The printed mezinha has the historical medicinal sense; this short continuation closes the plant entry.
The next Qicocu is returning to one’s own local country or domain, explicitly paraphrased cuniye cayeru. The Portuguese reino begins across rei-no and contrasts with Japan as a whole below.
Completes reino particular and gives Qicocu ſuru as the verb phrase. Por que then introduces the explanation distinguishing local return from return from abroad.

runs.text: tornar de outro reino eſtrãgeiro ao reino vniuer-

lines.note: The distinction concerns returning from a foreign country to the larger realm of Japan. The hyphen in vniuer- is visible and retained before the continuation.

runs.text: ſal de Iapão, ſe diz mais propriamente,

lines.note: Completes vniuerſal de Iapão, meaning Japan taken as the whole realm. The sentence says a different expression is more properly used; the name begins with capital I rather than OCR l.
Qichô ſuru supplies that preferred expression for returning to Japan from abroad. It is a standalone roman phrase continuing the Portuguese discussion, not a newly repeated headword.
The compound groups rising, being or sitting, activity, and stillness. The Japanese paraphrase continues with xizzu-cani; two z letters are visible, so the OCR’s single z is not retained.

Cani completes xizzucani xite iru, remaining quietly. There is no printed stop after cani; the Portuguese then begins rising, being, and working, with tra-balhar split over the row boundary. The provisional italic st in estar is retained.

runs.text: balhar, & eſtar quieto ſem ſemouer. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Completes trabalhar and being still without moving. The printed compact ſemouer is retained, and the abbreviation at the end has a tilde, Itẽ, introducing the additional temporal sense.

runs.text: Em todo tempo, ou ſempre. Vt,

lines.note: The added sense is at all times or always. Qicodô- begins the example using the compound in a phrase for the entire span of one’s activities.
Jǒno aida vaſurezu completes the example, not forgetting through all those activities. The Portuguese Lembrarſe ſempre em begins the same all-times interpretation.

Todo tempo completes remembering at all times. The final S. is an upright usage label, not part of the italic Portuguese sentence. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Qicon refers to constitution or mettle, rendered by calete and compreiſão. The repeated Qicon begins an example of a person with a strong constitution; the OCR’s gap after Q is removed.
No tçuyoi fito completes qicon no tsuyoi hito, a person strong in constitution or spirit. The Portuguese cõpreiſão retains its printed abbreviation rather than being modernized to compleição.

Qiconja, alternatively qiconxa, names a person of good constitution or mettle. The two roman Japanese alternatives are separated by the printed l, abbreviation, not treated as terms embedded in Portuguese.
Ou compreiſão completes the description of that person’s constitution. The final vowel marks are preserved as supplied; a small adjacent blemish is not expanded into an extra character.

runs.text: Homem que corta lenha nos matos.

lines.note: Qicori is a woodcutter, specifically a man cutting firewood in woodland. The initial Q belongs to the headword, and enlargement confirms the narrow printed space between corta and lenha.
Qicot combines the surface of the flesh and bones, paraphrased by hadaye and hone. The checked final t is retained; the Portuguese supplies the first part of the anatomical pair.

Adds bones to the flesh surface above. The final S. is an upright usage label; oßos keeps the printed double-s representation. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Qicoximeſare is an honorific verb covering hearing and consuming food or drink. The scan reads Ouuir with two u letters; the social restriction and third verb continue below.
Beber completes the list of actions, while peßoa honrada identifies the honored person performing them. It is not an instruction to drink a person or a gloss limited to hearing.
Qicoximexi has the same honorific senses, with its own principal parts. The initial letter is roman Q, replacing the isolated italic O in the OCR.
Qicoximexi ire means hearing and taking in something, said of a person of rank. The historical iruru principal part is retained, while the Portuguese nobility phrase continues across no-bre.
Completes nobre and adds perceiving or understanding something. This explains the added ire element in the honorific listening expression.

Qicoximexi voyobi is the honorific expression for hearing of or coming to hear something. The headword has o, not OCR u; enlargement confirms the printed circumflex in ôda. A later lexical check also lists this form: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. That corroboration does not replace the scan evidence.

runs.text: nobre algũa couſa, ou acertar de ouuir.

lines.note: The person of rank hears something or happens to hear it. This closes the honorific expression and the column, without an additional omitted example.
Qicoye is reputation or fame. The example begins a contrast between a good and a bad reputation; Qicoyega is a single roman word, not Q followed by a separate fragment.

runs.text: Soar bem, ou mal, ou auer boa, ou

lines.note: Varui completes the alternative to yoi. The Portuguese explains sounding good or bad, or having good or bad fame; the row visibly has the continuation indent.
Ruim fama completes the second alternative, a bad reputation. This is the short, indented close of the noun entry, not a new headword.
The verb Qicoye means being heard or becoming known. It is separate from the preceding noun despite the same citation form; its initial Q is not a detached word.
Qicoyevatari describes something becoming heard of far and wide. The Portuguese starts the geographical spread and is completed in the next row.

runs.text: muitas partes, ou ſer afamada a couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The thing is heard of in many places or becomes famous. Vt introduces the following example concerning a celebrated horse.
Miyaconi qicoye vatatta meibaga atta says there was a fine horse renowned in the capital. The printed separation qicoye vatatta is retained instead of being merged to match the headword.
Feiq. cites the Heike source, book 2. The Portuguese begins “there was a distinguished horse,” with inſigne split after inſig-; the citation label is roman and Lib. 2 is visibly italic.
Completes inſigne and says the horse was very famous in Miyako. Miaco is the Portuguese form of the capital’s name in the gloss, not a new Japanese headword.
Qicqei is joyful good fortune, paraphrased by yoki yorokobi. The Portuguese gives joy or pleasure, with prazer continued below.
Zer completes prazer. The separate upright S. is the usage label, outside the italic translation. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Qicqeô contrasts good and bad, explicitly paraphrased by yoshi and ashi. The circumflex is printed over the final o after e and is retained; S. is upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Qicqiǒ is a dung or latrine insect, paraphrased by funchū. The scan has c rather than OCR e, a caron on the final o, and caron-u in Funchǔ; Bicho and eſterco correct the corrupted Portuguese letterforms.

Latrinas finishes the insect gloss. Far to the right, the opening parenthesis marks displaced Outono, which semantically finishes the next row’s bonina do; both remain on this physical line rather than being reflowed into c2-l015.

Qicqua is the chrysanthemum flower, paraphrased by qicu no fana. The Portuguese reads “flower of autumn,” whose final Outono is printed at the far right of the preceding row; the scan has Qicqua, not Qiequa.

runs.text: Erua q̃ florece, ou dà flores no Outono.

lines.note: Qicu is a separate headword for the plant, described as flowering in autumn. The clear capital Q replaces OCR g, and the gloss reads dà flores rather than da ſtores; the visible grave is retained.
The same word Qicu can also name the flowers themselves, not just the plant. The compact printed meſmasflores is preserved without inserting an editorial word space.
Qicudaxi means putting clothing or armor on oneself. The headword is one roman word and its historical aita principal part is retained; veſti-do crosses the physical row boundary.
Completes veſtido and adds armor and similar equipment, placed upon oneself. It closes the dressing verb without an additional example.
Qicuguet and Qicuzzuqi are chrysanthemum-month names, equated with the ninth month. The synonym visibly contains zz, correcting Qicuazuqi; No- starts the Portuguese ordinal.
Na lũa completes nona lũa, the ninth lunar month. The tilde on u is preserved as printed rather than modernizing lua.
Qicumeixeqi names white stones from the shore with flowerlike markings. The visible sequence meixeqi replaces OCR meieqi; the compact q̃tem and abbreviation remain unexpanded.

runs.text: hũs ſinaes como boninas do Outono.

lines.note: The stones’ markings are compared to autumn flowers, continuing the chrysanthemum-related vocabulary. Hũs retains its printed abbreviation; the dark loop farther right belongs to damage, not the gloss.

Qicurague is the fungus kikurage, equated with mimitake. The scan clearly has Mimitaqe rather than Ximitaqe; the Portuguese reads Certa laya de cu-, with the mushroom word continued below despite nearby ink damage.
Gumelos completes the printed cu-gumelos, a kind of mushroom. The historical vowel in the first syllable is retained instead of regularizing it to modern cogumelos.
Qicuſui is chrysanthemum water, explicitly paraphrased by qicu no mizzu. The Japanese words remain roman; the Portuguese flower-water description continues across flo-res.

runs.text: res do Outono de que ſe falla em hũa fabula da

lines.note: The autumn-flower water is said to occur in a Chinese tale. Enlargement confirms the faint tilde on hũa; this row continues the particular legendary description, not a separate headword.

After completing China, the example introduces a chrysanthemum drinking gathering. The scan prints Qicuſu no yen with a space before no and no secure i after ſu; this is retained rather than normalized to the preceding headword Qicuſui.

runs.text: ſe faz aos noue dias da nona lũa metendo eſtas

lines.note: The gathering is held on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month, placing these flowers in the drink. The scan restores aos, dias, nona and eſtas from the corrupted OCR; lũa retains its visible tilde.
Boninas no vinho completes the description of putting flowers in wine. It is the close of the historical festival example rather than a separate botanical gloss.

runs.text: Pires, ou ſalſeiras de porſolana que

lines.note: Qicuzara denotes porcelain saucers or sauce dishes. The Japanese headword is joined after Q; the historical material spelling porſolana is retained.
The dishes bear pictures or patterns resembling flowers. This detail explains the chrysanthemum element of the headword and completes the porcelain entry.
Qicuzzuqi is the ninth lunar month, repeating the month name given as a synonym above. The double zz is retained in the roman Japanese form, and lũa retains its tilde.
Qidafaxi is a stair or stairway of stone or wood. The visible i after Q, omitted by OCR, is restored; the historical f represents the relevant Japanese h sound rather than a Portuguese long s.
Qidaruqi denotes wooden rafters or roof timbers. Enlargement confirms both dotted i letters in Aguieiros, so that unfamiliar Portuguese spelling is retained rather than shortened to Agueiros.

Qiden is a respectful second-person address, paraphrased by tattoqi tono. The final vowel in the divided title ſenhe-ria is damaged and open; the supplied e reading is retained provisionally rather than silently replacing it with the expected o of senhoria.
Ria completes the divided honorific title, followed by reuerencia and other respectful equivalents. It continues the address gloss and does not form another entry.
Qido is a gate or barrier, rendered by cancella. It is distinct from the next homophonous compound of emotions.
This Qido combines joy and anger, paraphrased by yorokobi and ikaru. The scan restores the o in Yorocobi and shows a hyphen after irar, joining to ſe below rather than ending a sentence.
Completes irarſe, then gives qido, airacu, the four emotions of joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure. The roman example has no word break after Q; the Portuguese enumeration continues below.
Triſteza and gozo complete the four-emotion list with sadness and delight. The row closes that example before the unrelated miraculous sense of Qidocu.
Qidocu is a wonder or miracle. The visible i in Marauilha corrects OCR Maraulha, while Qi- begins the repeated noun in the example on the following row.

runs.text: docuuo ſuru. l, naſu, guenzuru, arauaru.

lines.note: Docuuo completes qidocu wo, followed by suru and alternatives nasu, genzuru and arawaru. These are printed Japanese verb alternatives for doing or manifesting the wonder, not Portuguese terms requiring font toggles.
The Portuguese summarizes the alternatives as performing or manifesting miracles. The supplied provisional italic st classification in manifestar is retained.

Qidocuna is the attributive form, describing a marvelous or miraculous thing. The scan clearly supplies this headword and complete gloss in place of the heavily corrupted OCR; no new physical row is required.
Qidocuni is the corresponding adverbial form, printed alone and indented. Its blank remainder is genuine, not evidence of a lost Portuguese gloss.

Qidocuſa is the related noun of quality, marvelousness. The initial is Q rather than C and the consonant after u is a long s; the separately indented form ends the body text before the signature and catchword.
The far-right Qido- is a roman catchword below the body, separate from the centered signature. Its printed terminal hyphen is retained; the following page is outside this package.
